paragraphs.notes: B04-06 'rest in peace' -> 'live in peace'. Butler means an end of wandering and hardship (Homer 4.33-35, 'if ever Zeus would give us rest from misery hereafter'). In current English 'we may rest in peace' is the funerary formula, and tied to 'here, where…' it reads as a wish to die in the house. 'live in peace from now on' keeps 'in peace', 'from now on' and the prayer form 'heaven grant'. 'live' (= dwell) also fits Butler's contrast with staying at other people's houses. Butler's meaning is kept. 'live' does not occur elsewhere in Butler's ¶3, so there is no collision. Butler's 'rest' is current English, but the phrase no longer carries his meaning, which is the reason D29 asks for.

B04-07 'took nothing by it' -> 'gained nothing by it'. 'Take nothing by' (= gain nothing from) is obsolete. 'gain' is Butler's own verb for this idiom in the same Book (4 ¶38: 'you will gain nothing by trying to put me off'). It is also the accepted edition's rendering of Butler's identical 'he will take nothing by it' at 2 ¶10 ('he will gain nothing by it'). No collision: Butler's 'getting great riches' stays 'getting'. B04-09 'presently' -> 'then'. With a present-tense verb, 'presently' now reads as 'currently'. 'then' carries the sequence and 'again' carries the recurrence. Homer 4.102-103 has only 'at other times again I cease'. The 'soon' in Butler's 'presently' is still in the same sentence ('one soon tires of it'), so nothing is lost; 'before long' would be the literal alternative, but it is not needed. Neither 'then' nor 'gained' occurs elsewhere in ¶8. Butler's other two 'presently' in Book 4 (¶23 past narrative, ¶57 future) are confirmed and correctly kept.

B04-01: four 'should have' -> 'would have'. Butler's sense is a past counterfactual, not an obligation. (1) Homer 4.174-179 is unreal throughout: κε + aorist 'νάσσα … ἔτευξα' ('I would have settled … built'), κε + imperfect 'ἐμισγόμεθ᾽' ('we would have mingled'), 'οὐδέ κεν … διέκρινεν'. (2) Butler's own frame: the plan depended on 'when heaven had granted us a safe return', and the paragraph ends with heaven having 'prevented the poor fellow from ever getting home'. (3) Butler's 'nothing but death could have interrupted' continues the same unreal series. (4) Butler's paradigm is visible at 4 ¶28: 'We should have run clean out of provisions and my men would have starved, if a goddess had not…' (first-person should, third-person would, one conditional). In present-day English 'I should have founded a city for him' reads as 'I ought to have', so the fix is real. All four places change, so Butler's one construction stays one construction. Butler's ¶14 has no 'would' (no collision), 'could have interrupted' is untouched and nothing else changed. Not a defect of this edit: ¶28 keeps Butler's 'We should have run clean out…'. Its if-clause forces the counterfactual, so it does not need the same change.

B04-08 'paying their addresses to my mother' -> 'courting my mother'. The idiom is dead, and it carries the marriage suit that Menelaus answers in ¶27 ('usurp a brave man's bed', 'a sorry wedding'). 'courting' is Butler's word (6 ¶2, 13 ¶31, 18 ¶24, 24 ¶9, all verified). It is also the edition's accepted rendering of his near-identical line at 1 ¶16: Butler 'under the pretext of paying their court to my mother', edition 'on the pretext of courting my mother'. The same holds at 11 ¶7 and 16 ¶11 ('under the pretense of courting…'). Butler's 'pretence' (not 'pretext') stays 'pretense'. No collision.

B04-05 'A hind' -> 'A doe'. It is the same animal (female deer; Homer 4.335 ἔλαφος, feminine). 'doe' keeps the female that 'her new born young' needs, and nothing is added. The simile is otherwise unchanged. Butler has 'hind' only here and at 17 ¶10 (the repeat), both now 'doe', and the successor contains no 'hind' at all. ¶27 has no other doe or deer. Outside this edit: ¶27 keeps Butler's open 'new born' where 17 ¶10 prints 'newborn' (D15 would favor 'newborn'). This predates the change and is not a defect of it.

B04-02 'taken in water' -> 'taken in fresh water'. With vessels as the subject, 'have taken in water' now reads as leaking or swamped. Homer 4.359 ἀφυσσάμενοι μέλαν ὕδωρ means having drawn (drinking) water. Butler renders the same Greek verb at 9.85 as 'Here we landed to take in fresh water' (9 ¶4, verified), so 'fresh' restores his own phrase and adds nothing the source does not mean. The successor's other 'take in water' (10 ¶4, 'we went ashore to take in water') has people as the subject and cannot be read as a leak, so leaving it is consistent.

B04-10 'backed the wind' -> 'turned the wind back'. Butler's transitive nautical 'backed' now reads as 'supported'. 'turned … back' is Homer's verb (4.520 ἂψ … στρέψαν) and keeps Butler's meaning: the gods made the wind return to its former, fair direction, and they got home. His noun 'its old quarter' is kept. The alternative parse, 'turned the wind back into' (= made it revert to) 'its old quarter', gives the same sense. Only the nautical detail of a counterclockwise shift is lost, and that is not in Homer. No collision: Butler's 'return' ('he was to return safely') is a different word, and ¶42 has no other 'turn' or 'back'.

B04-03 'made sure' -> 'felt sure'. Butler's 'made sure' means 'felt certain' (Homer 4.639, οὐ γὰρ ἔφαντ᾽, 'they did not think'). In current English 'make sure that' means ensure or verify, which makes the suitors seem to have checked or arranged that he had not gone. 'felt sure' keeps Butler's 'sure' and changes only the verb. Butler's 'thought' in the next sentence stays distinct. The change is also needed for consistency with ¶57: leaving one of Butler's two identical phrases unrepaired would render it two ways in one Book. The kept 'make sure that Agamemnon did not give him the slip' at ¶43 is the live 'ensure' sense (Homer 4.526-527, he kept watch 'lest he slip past unseen'). Keeping it is correct, and the edition now separates Butler's two senses.

B04-04 'made sure' -> 'felt sure'. This is the same dead sense (Homer 4.664, φάμεν δέ οἱ οὐ τελέεσθαι, 'we thought it would not be accomplished'). Here, followed by 'but the young fellow has got away in spite of us', the 'ensure' reading makes the suitors seem to have acted to stop the voyage. 'felt sure' fixes that, with the same rendering as ¶54, and 'presently' in the next sentence is correctly kept. Advisory only, not a defect: Homer repeats this line at 16.346-347, and Butler prints the same words at 16 ¶31, where the edition has 'We were sure it would come to nothing'. Elsewhere the edition renders Butler's belief-sense 'made sure' as 'was sure' (13 ¶28, 16 ¶3, 17 ¶3). Both forms are correct. Harmonizing the two (e.g., 'we had been sure') is optional.

B04-12 'like sea-horses' -> 'like horses of the sea'. 'sea-horse' now names the fish, which makes no voyages. Homer 4.708-709 ἁλὸς ἵπποι, 'horses of the (salt) sea', means that ships are men's horses on the water. 'horses of the sea' opens Butler's compound into his and Homer's sense and adds nothing. Butler's 'like' is kept, and 'ocean' and 'sea' stay distinct words as in Butler. The reason says this rendering decision must be recorded in the continuity sheet (D15, PUNCTUATION §4). That record is not in the packet and could not be verified here. It is a records item, not a text defect.

B04-11. The clause had two real stumbles. The zero subject relative ('one of you would') is no longer standard, and 'giving me a call' now means telephoning. The edit supplies 'who' and turns Butler's noun 'call' into the verb 'calling', keeping his word (D29) and his sense (Homer 4.730 ἐκ λεχέων μ᾽ ἀνεγεῖραι, 'to rouse me from my bed'). 'called out of bed' is idiomatic current English for being woken or summoned. Butler's other 'call' in ¶64 ('call old Dolius') is also 'summon', as in Butler, so there is no collision. The quotation structure is unchanged (one opening and one closing double quote, as in BEFORE).

summary: Mechanical (own script v417/mech417.py): BEFORE sha256 bd05c7f43da64bfe…afc9c confirmed; AFTER successor-b3456-17.json sha256 22b34077dd19cc5a…; structure identical: 24 chapters, 1,027 paragraphs, identical chapter numbers, titles and per-chapter counts, top-level keys identical. Books differing anywhere in the file: 3, 4, 5, 6, 17 only (3/5/6 not reviewed here). Book 4 (81 paragraphs): exactly ¶3, 8, 14, 26, 27, 28, 42, 54, 57, 61 and 64 differ, which is the packet set. Applying the 12 listed edits (B04-01 to B04-12) to BEFORE reproduces AFTER exactly in every paragraph. Each old string occurs exactly once, and there is no unlisted edit. The packet's BEFORE, AFTER and CONTEXT texts match the files verbatim. The packet's BUTLER texts match the served original-en at the same index after whitespace normalization (the served file keeps PG's hard line breaks). Conventions hold in all 11 AFTER paragraphs: no straight quotes, no 'towards', no spaced dashes, American spelling, and quote counts identical to BEFORE. Verdicts: 11 of 11 VERIFIED CLEAN, 0 defects. The four 4 ¶14 conditionals are counterfactual in Butler and Homer, so 'would have' is right. 'felt sure' (¶54, ¶57) and the kept live 'make sure' (¶43) now separate Butler's two senses correctly. 'live in peace' (¶3) and 'turned the wind back' (¶42) keep Butler's meaning. Advisory, outside this packet: 9 ¶36 in the successor still prints Butler's belief-sense 'we made sure it had been the death of us' (Homer: 'we thought we would perish there'), the same dead sense that B04-03 and B04-04 repair. OVERALL: VERIFIED CLEAN.
